title: What the parties say on religion and state
question: Who should run marriage, conversion and Shabbat rules?
note: Shas and UTJ rows quote the Jerusalem Post's summary of the two parties' positions, and the Yashar row the Jewish Chronicle's; neither is the party's own text. Religious Zionism–Zehut, Blue and White, Likud and the Joint List rows use their answers to Ynet on Shabbat transport (Aug 31, 2026). Likud has not said where it stands on marriage or conversion; its row is marked not said publicly and rests on its coalition deals and the laws its government passed. Otzma Yehudit's row is its leader's 2022 statement; Noam's comes from israel2026.co.il, an aggregator site. No position found for People of Israel, Reservists–Economic or Ra'am, and the Joint List's answer does not fit these options (checked October 2026); their rows give older or adjacent material, which sets no stance.

rows.text: Jerusalem Post summary of Shas and UTJ: "They have firmly opposed expanding alternatives to religious law, including civil marriage"; on conversion they "favor keeping the authority to do so within the Orthodox religious establishment"; they "oppose changes that would expand non-Orthodox forms of worship at the Western Wall." Shas championed the July 2026 law returning kosher certification to the Chief Rabbinate (Times of Israel).
Same positions as Shas in the Jerusalem Post summary. MK Moshe Gafni, sponsor of the Torah study Basic Law: "This Basic Law will serve as the state's moral compass."

Has not said where it stands on marriage or conversion. On marriage its coalition deal with UTJ keeps the religious status quo, but Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana of Likud voted for a civil marriage bill on Dec 24, 2025, and Likud MK Dan Illouz defended him. On Shabbat transport it told Ynet it wants "to connect Israel on the six working days while keeping Shabbat," holding to the status quo since the state's founding (translated). Its 2022 coalition deal with Religious Zionism recognizes only conversions under the Orthodox Chief Rabbinate, and its government passed the Shas law restoring the Rabbinate's exclusive control of kosher certification, 46 to 41, on Jul 15, 2026.
rows.source: Times of Israel, Jul 15, 2026; Ynet (Hebrew), Aug 31, 2026; Times of Israel, Dec 28, 2022

rows.text: Itamar Ben-Gvir in 2022: "The state is Jewish; marriages should be according to the law of Moses and Israel" (translated). Its published platform says nothing on marriage, conversion or Shabbat. Its MK Limor Son Har-Melech sponsored the July 2026 law allowing gender-segregated graduate programs.
rows.source: Arutz Sheva (Hebrew), Sep 7, 2022; Times of Israel, Jul 16, 2026

rows.text: On Shabbat transport, Religious Zionism told Ynet it opposes any change, saying that keeping Shabbat in public life expresses Israel's character as a Jewish state (Ynet's summary, translated). Its 2022 coalition deal provides that "only conversions performed by the state conversion court under the auspices of the Orthodox Chief Rabbinate will be granted state recognition" (Times of Israel).
rows.source: Ynet (Hebrew), Aug 31, 2026; Times of Israel, Dec 28, 2022

rows.text: "Preserving Shabbat in public space and strengthening the Orthodox rabbinate, conversion and kashrut." Its leader, Avi Maoz, sponsored the Western Wall bill.

The Jewish Chronicle's summary: "a secular party, but not anti-religious" that "supports civil marriage, divorce and same-sex marriage," with a "'live and let live' approach to Shabbat observance, devolving decisions to municipalities." Eisenkot (Jerusalem Post, Sep 24, 2026): "I am not religious, but I grew up in a traditional family and have profound respect for Judaism and tradition."

Lapid: "In the State of Israel, there should be a parallel civil marriage option for anyone who wants it," with legislation on equal rights for every couple sought within the first 100 days of the next government (Sep 15, 2026). Bennett, Apr 20, 2026, before the B'Yachad merger: "We should allow cities to choose whether they want public transportation on Shabbat."

"Promote civil marriage"; "promote the operation of public transport on Shabbat in a limited format in secular localities"; "extend recognition of conversion to other religious bodies in addition to the Chief Rabbinate."

"We will demand the implementation of civil marriage and divorce options within Israel"; "Tel Aviv will not impose Shabbat transportation on Bnei Brak, and Bnei Brak will not impose its way of life on Tel Aviv"; the Western Wall compromise as drafted by Avichai Mandelblit and Natan Sharansky.

No position found on marriage, conversion, Shabbat or the Rabbinate. The party's founding principles call for "a state where Judaism invites and does not coerce, includes and does not dictate" (translated).
rows.source: People of Israel, founding principles (Hebrew, undated)

rows.text: Benny Gantz backs public transport on Shabbat as part of handing powers to local authorities, which would set routes and frequency (Ynet, translated). No 2026 statement on marriage found. In 2019 it pledged to "legislate the partnership covenant," a civil union for couples who want one, while calling marriage by Jewish tradition "the main road of the Jewish people" (translated).
No position found for the list. Yoaz Hendel, as communications minister in 2021: "We must provide an alternative for those unable to marry" (translated).

Told Ynet it supports urban and intercity public transport on Shabbat, including the airport and hospitals, "as a basic and equal service for the whole population" (translated). No joint 2026 position on marriage or conversion found. Hadash's platform, as quoted in 2019, calls for "separation of religion from state" and civil marriage and divorce (translated).

No position found on marriage, conversion or Shabbat. Mansour Abbas, on cutting the party's ties with its religious council: "Ra'am today is moving in the direction of being a completely civic party, with separate institutions."
